utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. The affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies. If you could please sit down. And Ms. Kravetz continues.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I have very few questions left for you, so I hope we are going to conclude your testimony quite quickly this morning. Sir, yesterday, we spoke quite at length about the action called Reka in the Carragojs and Trava valley; do you recall we went over that in quite some detail yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, during the course of this trial, we have heard evidence that during the course of this action Reka, hundreds of Kosovo Albanian civilians who lived in the area of the Carragojs valley and Trava valley were expelled from their homes by members of units who participated in this action. Do you have any information on that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have information to the effect that the action took place, but civilians certainly were not a target for expulsion. The basic aim of that action was to destroy the Siptar terrorist forces. The civilian population was certainly no target of any kind of abuse, expulsion included.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We also have evidence, sir, in this case, that members of the units who participated in this action killed around 300 civilians, men and boys, during the course of this action. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, there was talk about that; I read about it later. But I do not have any immediate knowledge from that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say "later on there was talk about that," which period are you referring to that you heard talk about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after 2000, say in the year 2001. As the book appeared, the one that I mentioned yesterday, "Kosovo, As Seen, As Told." Before that, I had not heard anything or seen anything about that, or did I have any direct evidence least of all. The only information I had with regard to that event was based on that book and things that were written in the press, and they were probably written on the basis of that book actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yesterday, sir, when we were discussing one of your statements you gave to the commission for co-operation regarding the Cerim district, you told me that a small part of your unit, a maximum of 20 men, were based at a wine cellar some 400, 500 metres from the Cerim district. Do you remember giving that evidence yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that, approximately. That many, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, we have heard testimony in this case that some of the men captured during action Reka were held at a wine cellar in the area of the Cerim district, and that these men later disappeared and have not since -- have not been heard from or seen since. Do you know anything about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you not hear anything from any of your subordinates about men, Kosovo Albanian men, being held in a wine cellar in the area of the Cerim district? You got no reports about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The members of my unit spent a very short period of time at that particular locality. They were on the move all the time, so they spent a little bit of time there as well. So I have no knowledge of that, and it is impossible that these people were there at the same time when my soldiers were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I see, sir. Sir, we also have evidence indicating that the bodies of some of the persons of the victims of this Reka action were buried at the Rekovac [phoen] cemetery right outside Djakovica. Do you know anything about that? Did you hear anything at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing, I heard nothing about that. This is the first information I received about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In your contacts with the Djakovica SUP or the president of the municipality you heard nothing? No one told you anything?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one ever told me anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And, sir, we have also witness testimony and forensic evidence in this case that shows that the remains of the persons who were killed in this action Reka were found at a mass grave in the firing range of Batajnica outside of Belgrade. Do you have any information on that? Do you know anything about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that from the press, just like I found out about that previous information. So this was written about in Belgrade at that same time, after 2000, when that book appeared. Before that, I did not know a thing about any of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You would agree with me, sir, that 300 bodies is quite a large number of bodies to move all the way to the Batajnica firing range outside of Belgrade, wouldn't you, sir? This is quite a large number of bodies; you would require quite some organisation and planning to move such a large number of bodies from Djakovica municipality all the way to a locality outside of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that if that is indeed the case, that is a complicated operation, and a very unusual one. It -- to my mind, it is quite incredible, and that is why I can hardly believe that that kind of thing crossed anyone's mind at the time, let alone carried it out. If someone indeed did carry that out, they must have known exactly when the NATO air force would strike and when it would not strike. At that time, NATO air force was striking all the time, including at passenger vehicles, privately owned. So that story is quite unbelievable as far as I'm concerned. And what is even more unbelievable for me is that someone transported such a large number of corpses that far away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you are saying, sir, that at the time you heard nothing about any transfer of bodies from the municipality where you were based to a locality outside of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing, nothing. I had no idea about that. No idea whatsoever until the press started writing about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, during the course of your testimony yesterday and the previous day as well, you were shown portions of the statement of one of your former subordinates Nike Peraj and you went -- and you were asked to comment on portions of the statement; do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you recall, sir, that repeatedly you said, when my learned colleague was reading out to you portions of Mr. Peraj's statement, you -- your responses were that the portions that were read out to you were not true, contained lies, were pure fabrications? Do you recall giving those answers yesterday, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answers were that most of the statements were incorrect. There were also some that were correct, inter alia that I was brigade commander and that he was in this brigade, that we were in Djakovica. So not all of his answers were incorrect. Most of the answers contained in his statements were incorrect. If you remember, that is what I had actually said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm not going to put to you each one of the responses that you gave to my learned colleague, but I recall, sir, that you did not only say that some of the answers were incorrect, in fact, you said that these were pure lies, fabrications, that what Mr. Peraj was saying was not true. Do you recall saying that, sir? You spoke about lies and fabrications?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me an incorrect thing and a lie are one in the same thing. If you say that something is incorrect, that means that the person who uttered that uttered a lie. I don't see any difference really between incorrect and a lie.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: One of the portions of the statement that was put to you is paragraph 95 which says: "Dosan," and that's a reference to you, "did not agree with the operation in Korenica and Meja and arrested Micunovic for his involvement in it. However, Micunovic was released some three days later." And your response to that was that none of this is true. Do you recall giving that answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that was the answer I gave and that is what I assert. I did not arrest Micunovic; I am not aware of Micunovic having been in prison; and I'm not aware of his being set free by a man of Seselj's or whatever, or whoever he mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You maintain, sir, that you have no knowledge of what transpired during the course of this operation in Korenica and Meja?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had knowledge that pertained to my own unit, which was, after all, my duty to have that knowledge, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us about your career as an officer in the VJ, and I take it, sir, that given your vast experience as a soldier, you are quite familiar with the laws of war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Of course I am aware of the laws of war, and I insisted upon that all the time. I transmitted that knowledge and experience to my subordinates; I gave them orders to abide by that; and we familiarised the soldiers to the extent to which it is relevant for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Given your experience and knowledge in the laws of war, sir, you would agree with me that the deliberate killing of civilians in an armed conflict by either members of the army or of the police constitutes a war crime?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, especially if it is being committed deliberately, intentionally, by inhumane means. Of course. Any killing is problematic. The killing of civilians in particular. Every war is problematic as well, so I think that that is an answer that you can get from anyone. No one has to be an eminent expert in humanitarian law in order to be able to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And as an officer with a long career in the VJ, you wouldn't want to have any involvement with an action that led to the commission of a war crime, sir, would you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an officer of the Army of Yugoslavia, I would never allow a crime to be committed; I would particularly not allow my units that I command. I condemn every crime, and I would report any crime to my superiors regardless of who might have committed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And can I take from that answer, sir, that you would, in fact, do everything possible or that you could do to distance yourself from any action, military action, that involved the commission of a war crime?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I distance myself from any crime and any act that results in a crime, so you can consider that to be my answer. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And, sir, if an order to distance yourself from the commission or from an action that led to the commission of a war crime like the one I have been referring here today, the killing of 300 men, if an order to distance yourself from such an action, if that would involve coming here to discredit a former VJ colleague of yours, Captain Nike Peraj, you would do that, sir, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand your question. Of course I distance myself from any crime. Not a single one of our actions was planned in such a way so as to know that there would ultimately be a crime committed, and I would not take part in any such thing. If you think that we commanders who took part in that action knew or thought in advance that a crime would be committed, then it's not fair on your part. Crimes were never planned. Actions were never planned that included crimes. Actions were always planned only to fight against terrorist forces, or, rather, to engage air targets. That is what the air defence specifically did. Specifically not a single action was ever planned with the intention of it including a crime. That is totally wrong. It is totally wrong to say that. And I can energetically state that I and anyone else from the army would distance himself from that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: My question was a bit more specific, sir. You said, Of course I distance myself from any crime. If, in order to distance yourself from such a crime like the one we've been speaking about today, you had to come here to The Hague and discredit the testimony given by a former VJ colleague of yours, Nike Peraj, you would do that, sir, wouldn't you, in order to distance yourself from this crime?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I gave my statement here with regard to the allegations made by him, I think that in that way, I am discrediting his statement, what he said. I don't see what else you mean by distancing myself or discreditation. I'm saying that what he said was not correct. I distance myself in this way from him and from his statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you're saying that, sir, because you do not want to be seen in any way linked to any crimes that may have taken place during action Reka; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course that no one can link me in any way with alleged crimes anywhere, action Reka included, if these crimes actually did take place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for your answers, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, I would like to go back to the 24th of March. Can you tell us what Major Odak said to you about Katolicka Street and whether he had seen anything personally?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that he saw the rocket fall or the cruise missile, it's hard to see. It was night-time and it's hard to see when the speed is so big, but he did see the projectile fall in Katolicka Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the projectile fell, did a fire break out in that street?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since I was in shelter, I heard this, I didn't see it. But soon afterwards, Katolicka Street was ablaze.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you spoke about refugees that were passing by in waves, as you had said, in the beginning of April. I think that remained unclear, so my question to you is were these refugees from the town of Djakovica or from other areas in Kosovo-Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained, as I was showing the map, where the NATO air force was striking, and it is certain that refugees from Djakovica, that is to say, those who were closer to the border, and those from Prizren too, that they appeared sooner or faster at the Albanian border. The others were assembling there, those coming from far away places. They were mostly moving on tractor or on foot. They assembled in certain areas. From time to time, they were hindered by air-strikes. Very often bridges were destroyed on the roads that they took. So even if they wanted to, they could not have arrived at the same time when the refugees from Djakovica or specifically Prizren, but since I'm talking about Djakovica, when they arrived at that territory. It is only natural that those who have to take the longest road are going to take the longest period of time to reach their objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My learned friend quoted General Petkovic's statement to you, and you said that you knew him. But she only quoted a certain part of the statement. I'm going to quote another part of that statement. Paragraph 6. Do you know that General Petkovic used ammunition containing depleted uranium from the 30th of March onwards?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know General Petkovic. I'm not aware of his statement. I did not look at his statement. However, I was down there; I saw those aircraft appear. They appeared there towards the end of March. That is aircraft carrying that kind of ammunition only. On the other hand, it is a readily recognisable type of aircraft by its form and by the sound it generates. You don't even have to see an A-10, you can hear it. It has a special kind of engines. Also it has a special kind of purpose. It is intended to instill fear in people, just like the Stuka aircraft in the Second World War had that function. The A-10 had that same purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now I would like to deal with the following: A part of your statement in the Milosevic [as interpreted] case on page 45436 was quoted to you when you said why operation Reka was started. However, on page 45438 of the same transcript, you still speak about operation Reka and the reasons why they were taken, and you say, This area where operation Reka took place was the area where a land aggression is -- was supposed to take place. That was Normandy for the terrorists. So were those the reasons that you mentioned as the reasons for starting or launching operation Reka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Those were the basic reasons. And I claim to this day that that is what the beach head or the bridge head was supposed to be, and the terrorists were supposed to start from there in order to continue their journey as a land aggression. I used these picturesque terms. I said at that time that Reka was indeed what Normandy was for opening the second front on the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Yesterday you were shown P1540, the statement of Lieutenant-Colonel Zlatko Odak of the 26th of December, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see that document now, page 2 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, in the second paragraph, Zlatko Odak states as follows: "As far as I recall, I took the seal-off line with the company at 630 hours and we were 30 minutes behind schedule because there was a delay in fully establishing a linkup between the platoons in the company and with the neighbours to the left and right." When it says that they were 30 minutes behind schedule, what does that actually mean? According to that, when did the Reka action start?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It started at 600 hours on the 27th of April, 1999. He arrived somewhat later to the start position, or, as he refers to it, the seal-off line. The action was planned to start at 600 hours on the 27th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, tell us how long on that day were you in the company of General Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I left the ceremony at around 1300 hours since my positions were the furthest. Some commanders who were stationed closer to Pristina stayed for a bit longer, but I was the first to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. If a corps commander is coming to the forward command post, would you be advised of that, and was there a possibility that the Chief of Staff and the corps commander be in the same location during war time operations?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this would not be customary, and it certainly would be un-wise. They are never in the same place, for security reasons. Also, they are not supposed to ride in the same vehicle at the same time or be in the same place. There were constant NATO air-strikes, and they could have been hit at any point in time. And in that case, if they were together, the corps would in one go be left without the commander and the Chief of Staff. We applied the same principle in my unit. Myself and my Chief of Staff were basically never in the same location together, for the very reason of the possibility that if the commander is killed, the Chief of Staff is the one who is supposed to assume command.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, let's go back to operation Meja. Was this a wider-ranging operation? Was it bigger in terms of size? Because you have already explained the difference between an action and operation.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Action Meja was important and necessary, but it was not a wide-ranging action neither by the amount of forces nor by its length in terms of time. It was necessary to undertake it, but that area did not require a great deal of forces or prolonged periods of time of engagement of those forces in that action. It was a forested terrain for the most part, and more lethal assets could not be used there. One could only use lighter weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Do you know what duties Nike Peraj performed in the VJ while he was its member?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nike Peraj was in my unit where he was officially appointed as the desk officer of the operations section of the staff. I also know that the chief of security engaged him according to his plans. Security organs are entitled to do so. On several occasions, my chief of security when I asked him where are you taking Peraj, he would say, Commander, he's been an associate of ours for quite some time. And, as a rule, commanders did not try to interfere with that part of the work. I know that he collaborated with the security organ, and, among others, that was one of the reasons why he was transferred to Djakovica. He was brought closer to home as a way of rewarding him for the assistance he offered to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you. I shall try to be as brief as possible. Now, you commanded the 52nd ARBR of the VJ stationed in Djakovica. Now, did you have any reservists under your command at all? Any reservists?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, there were reservists. Reservists are soldiers, people who are kept in the reserve until such time when they are called to join a unit. As of the moment they joined a unit, they are no different to anyone else in terms of their rights, duties, or insignia. They belong to that part of the defence system which is dormant in peacetime. Once a war is underway, they are mobilised into units, becoming their integral part. And as of that moment, they are no longer reservists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In slang terms, they were usually referred to as such. But the truth is that they were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now, you said that there were no paramilitaries in Djakovica, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of Arkan's Tigers at all? Arkan's Tigers?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of Arkan's Tigers after the war, there was much discussion and writing about it, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: For example, during the war when you were in Djakovica, did you hear of them at all, Arkan's Tigers?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Seselj's White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Or Frenki's men?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I neither heard of them at that time nor seen them at the time. I had no information of them being accommodated anywhere in the town of Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now, you said that some things in Peraj's statement were incorrect and some were correct, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that most of Peraj's statement is incorrect and that only small portions are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now, is it correct that in March, after the NATO bombing started, you refused the request of a group of 50 men to stay in Djakovica saying that you would not allow them to loot? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I see. Now, again, you said you saw refugees coming in waves, groups of 200 to 300 to 350, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Okay. And they would gather or assemble at a particular place, wait from -- for one another, and they would then continue their journey together; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are. I never saw individual families moving about. They mostly moved in columns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Splendid. Now, were these people escorted by forces of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Were they escorted at all?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I see. Were there any check-points set up at all along the way?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no check-points along their routes. There were check-points in certain locations to control the traffic, but they were not there for the sake of the refugees. The check-points had existed prior to the mass exodus. They were not set up for them or because of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you gave reasons as to why they were leaving Djakovica, you gave three reasons, basically. And very briefly I'll run through them. You said the first was fear of indiscriminate and persistent NATO bombing, especially fear of ammunition containing depleted uranium; that was the first basic reason you gave, agreed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the principle reason. It was one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Right, one reason, fair enough. The other reason was, again, I would summarise, fear of cross-fire?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But that was another reason, good. And the third reason you gave was persistent propaganda and fear of retaliation if they did not move out?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now, then, I want some clarification as to what followed. You said the situation was such that a normal person could hardly take it. You said: "I'm an air force officer, and I was afraid. There were soldiers who did not dare leave shelter." Are you with me so far?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: You said: "Fear is a normal phenomenon, especially for those who do not know and who cannot seek shelter or mask themselves and take other measures in order to protect themselves from air-strikes."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But, now, I'm a bit confused because are you joining the first reason to the third reason?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what is confusing you. What I can tell you is that it is normal to feel fear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not -- no. You gave the first reason as fear of indiscriminate and persistent NATO bombing, and the third reason as persistent propaganda and fear of retaliation if they did not move out. But then you continued on and you spoke of you were afraid there were soldiers who did not dare leave shelter. And then you said it is a "phenomenon, especially for those who do not know ... who cannot seek shelter or mask themselves and take other measures in order to protect themselves from [shelter]." Now, shelter was the first reason, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that the first reason was the fear of bombing, which was persistent and indiscriminate. Then the fear of being caught in cross-fire because the terrorists, once NATO air-strikes began, revealed themselves abruptly and began attacking our units. It was actually a co-operation of the terrorists and NATO aviation. The units which were supposed to engage NATO aircraft were constantly being exposed to terrorist attacks. As the commander, I can tell you that NATO aircraft killed three of my soldiers. Fourteen were killed by terrorists from the ground as the soldiers were trying to fend off the aircraft. There was direct co-operation between NATO aviation and the terrorists on the ground. They helped each other. In military parlance it is called co-operation and support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have one last question for you. Now, you referred to paragraph 97 of Nike Peraj's statement and you said that: "Nike Peraj gave that evidence before the court because he was in a situation where he had to choose between truth on one hand and life on the other." You were convinced that: "He was forced into doing that and he had no choice, he was either to say that or to lose someone close to him." Do you recollect saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But my question is this: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read Nike Peraj's statement. He said that he was on the list of those who were supposed to be killed by the KLA. He also said that immediately after leaving the VJ, military police came for him and took him to KLA headquarters. With the assistance of NATO, the KLA moved into certain areas because they lay low previously to that. Once NATO aircraft began engaging us, they began attacking full force. Even without him saying so, it would only be logical that he be exposed to threats because he was with the unit throughout the period from the beginning until the end of the war. He was a member of the army throughout. To them it meant he was with the enemy. Although we were the official armed force of that state, they treated us as enemies. That is how they behaved. They opened fire on us, they kidnapped our personnel, killed our personnel. Those who were part of enemy formation were eventually to be brought under pressure or under their law, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Those were the two sources that you derive this information from?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DOSAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what a third source could be more convincing than that, than him saying that he was on the list to be shot. He was supposed to be liquidated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will be pleased to know that that concludes the questions. The Chamber would thank you for your attendance in The Hague and for the assistance you have been able to give. You may, of course, now return to your normal activities, and a Court Officer will show you out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before we call the next witness, I would like to use this opportunity, when my learned friend Ms. Gopalan is present, to notify the Court that we have prepared D510, which is derived from the testimony of Witness Gojevic [phoen], according to your instruction. We forwarded that notification to the OTP, and I believe we are in agreement as to what that document should look like in keeping with the suggestions of the witness. I have here the ERN number, it is D011-2257, which is actually D510.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And that will now be incorporated in the transcript as the Exhibit D510. I notice it's in the transcript page 20, line 9, as D150, it should be D510; is that correct? Thank you very much for that, both of you. Now, the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please read the affirmation aloud that's shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir, Colonel Filipovic. For the sake of the transcript, please tell us your first and last name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Milutin Filipovic. Father's name: Slobodan. I was born on the 25th of November, 1948, in Pristina. That is it concerning my personal data.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, on the 27th and 28th of November, 2007, you testified in the Milutinovic case before this Tribunal. If I put the same questions to you today, would you provide the same answers? This Defence has enabled you to reread your previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would provide practically the same answers as I did on the 27th and 28th of November, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that transcript is number D010-1920. Could we please have that brought up. I seek to tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be received as Exhibit D00712. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether you can hear what I'm saying actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We can, Mr. Djurdjic, especially when your light is on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would now like to present the summary of witness Milutin Filipovic. The witness was born in 1948 in Pristina, is now a retired colonel of the VJ. During 1998 and 1999, the witness held the post of deputy commander of the Pristina Corps in charge of personnel and housing matters. In the period of 1986 to 1992, he had performed various duties in the bodies of the Territorial Defence of the Autonomous Province of Kosovo-Metohija. As of the 29th of March, 1999, by order of the commander of the Pristina Corps, in addition to his regular duties, he was appointed head of the group of the command of the Pristina Corps in the Pristina garrison. The witness was head of the command group as well as provisional commander of the Pristina garrison. The witness will also speak about the period of aggression against the FRY and Kosovo-Metohija during 1999, about the non-combat parts of the Pristina Corps, such as the military court, the clinic, the library, et cetera. Also about the deployment and activities of non-combat groups of the Army of Yugoslavia that were in Pristina, and the surrounding area. Also, he will speak of the attitude of the Army of Yugoslavia towards the civilian population. The witness will speak about the deployment and locations of the command of the Pristina Corps during the war in 1999. He will present his knowledge about the activity of terrorist forces during 1998 and 1999, with special reference to the territory of the town of Pristina and the surrounding area. He will particularly explain the situation in the villages outside Pristina on the immediate eve of the war and during the war itself, namely 1998 and 1999, like the villages of Ajvalija, Maticane, Susice, et cetera. Also about the city neighbourhoods of Vranjevac, Dragodan, and so on. The witness will present his knowledge to the effect that there were no deportations or expulsions in Pristina or the surrounding area. He will familiarise us with the functioning of public institutions and public utilities during the war, especially from the point of view of social welfare, food supplies, medical care for the population, et cetera; also, radio and TV station broadcasts, printed media, and the functioning of religious places of worship in Pristina. He will tell us about the situation in Pristina and the surrounding area during air-raids. He will tell us about the locations where that happened, and it's effect on the life of civilians in Pristina. He will also tell us about terrorist activities during the war. He will make us aware of the personal contacts he had with civilians during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you and I speak the same language. I would like to ask you to speak at a pace that will make it possible for the interpreters to do their job so that we could all have an accurate transcript, and that is the aim of your testimony, to be recorded correctly in the transcript. I will take care to do the same thing. You are now a retired colonel. Could you tell us, briefly, what work you did before you retired and when it was that you retired?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can, as briefly as possible. I will tell you which positions I held. Like many officers, after I completed the military academy, I was first commander of a platoon and then a platoon in the military police, then I was company commander in the military police, then assistant battalion commander for morale in the military police. Then I was operations officer in a brigade, operations officer in a zone staff of the Territorial Defence, of Pristina that is. Then commander of the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Pristina, and assistant commander of the Pristina Corps for personnel issues and mobilisation, assistant commander of the Pristina Corps for personnel matters, and later on assistant commander for personnel in housing matters. The positions that you also mentioned during your summary, the positions I held during the aggression, and that would be it. After that, I served for another three years in the guards brigade, and then I retired in 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me, briefly, up until the 29th of March, 1999, which position did you hold in Pristina -- in the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I was assistant commander of the Pristina Corps for personnel and housing matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D006-2525. Your Honour, if you allow me, we'd like to give the witness a binder containing hard copies of the documents that we will use so that we could work more efficiently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, number 1, we see it on our screens now. This is an order of the command of the Pristina Corps dated the 30th of March, 1999. It has to do with the establishment of a group within the corps command. We see, under number 1, that you were appointed leader of that group and temporary commander of the Pristina garrison as well. I would now like to ask you to tell us briefly what the elements were within that group that was established on the basis of this order?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as you can see from this document, this group was rather comprehensive. It included an organ for garrison affairs and the entire organ for personnel and housing affairs; the entire section for presenting the situation in air-space; parts of the operation centre; the chief of air surveillance and warning; parts of the information technology office; the entire military orchestra; the military club; the military library; the Military Prosecutor's Office; the military court; and then some other smaller groups at a later point in time. This is an order I received orally, and it had to do with smaller groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were your duties as the temporary or provisional commander of the Pristina garrison?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: My duties as temporary commander of the Pristina garrison were prescribed by the rules of service, especially a chapter that had to do with the garrison and the duties of garrison commander. I think it's on page 51 in the rules of service and around that page. These duties primarily entailed ensuring order and discipline, the proper functioning of services within the garrison, and overall life and work in the garrison that is prescribed by the rules of service. I don't want to go into all of them individually. There are quite a few of them, and they are rather complex. That is what I think I should say at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us how many people were in this command group that you headed?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This command group had about 150 to 200 people, sometimes more, sometimes less; but as the aggression progressed, the group became bigger. Personnel levels particularly went up in the field of food supplies, but basically it's the figure that I mentioned originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us about the weapons that the members of your group had and what kind of uniforms they wore?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Their weapons were prescribed by the war establishment of the command of the Pristina Corps. It was basically light infantry weapons, that is to say, pistols and rifles. Uniforms of the Army of Yugoslavia were worn, those that were according to regulations at the time in accordance with the rules and regulations that governed military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From the beginning of the war until the end of the war did, the members of your command group engage in any kind of combat activity?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From the beginning of the aggression, or, more precisely, from the 24th of March onwards until the Kumanovo Agreement was reached, the members of our command group and the Pristina garrison were not engaged in any combat activity whatsoever or were there any armed conflicts that they took part in. Namely, we did not fire a single bullet or did we point a gun at anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you suffer any casualties during the course of the war? I'm referring to your command group, the one that you headed.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From the beginning until the end of the aggression, like many units of the Pristina Corps, our group sustained losses as well. We had had two fatalities, and three of our members were wounded. It was an NCO who got killed, Izderic, Slavisa; the Siptar terrorists killed him. And Dejan Vitorevic [phoen], a soldier, was killed by NATO air-strikes. Three members of the group were wounded; two officers and one soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What were their duties when they were killed or wounded? What was the work that they were involved in?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, basically they were going about their regular duties. Slavisa Izderic, that non-commissioned officer, was a member of the military orchestra. At the time when he got killed, he was passing through the neighbourhood of Vranjevac. Siptar terrorists fired at him; he was killed; and we could not find his body because the terrorists took him away, as an eye-witness told us. And a civilian of Serb ethnicity was wounded there. To this day, his mortal remains, Slavisa Izderic's mortal remains, have not been found, although we immediately went to the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the others wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Vitorevic was killed close to his house in Pristina, close to the municipal building. As the military conscript, he asked me for leave to go home during that night, and he was then killed in his house after NATO airplane struck the postal building and the residential area around the post office during the night between the 6th and the 7th of April, 1999. As for the other two officers and one soldier, they were wounded by the Siptar terrorists from fire-arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the document before us, we see that there were groups, subgroups, formed among which there was a subgroup of the Military Prosecutor's Office and the military court. What was the relationship between the corps command group and the group of the military judiciary or organs?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The corps command vis-à-vis these two important bodies of the corps, that is, the Military Prosecutor's Office and the military court, had a fair relationship from the start. These two organs in terms of how they operated were completely independent. And, as far as I know, they performed their duties in accordance with the law and first and foremost the constitution, and the Law on Armed Forces as well as the Law on Military Courts and other relevant regulation regulating the competencies and duties of military courts and military prosecutors. Neither myself nor anyone else from the command group or from the Pristina garrison command exerted no influence whatsoever upon their work. We only tried to provide sufficient security so that they could work during the period they existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This securing of conditions for the work, what did that entail?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, it was on different levels and it differed from one period to the next. I can state a few of our duties because they were numerous. We, for example, secured the building where they were housed. We provided them with work conditions in the sense that we secured premises, logistics, food, shower, as well as assisted them in summoning jurors and bringing them in the building. This was a very complex task, because some jurors had to come from areas where Siptar terrorists were active. We also secured them en route. We provided communication inside the building, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what the technical composition was of the military court and the Military Prosecutor's Office during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, their composition reflected the ethnic makeup of the Pristina Corps as well as the entire country to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were any Albanians in the Military Prosecutor's Office and military court in Pristina during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Individually speaking, I don't remember everyone from the court, but I think there were, although I can't tell you which part of the institution they belonged to. I think, and as far as I can recall, there were some Siptars, especially among technical personnel and those who provided translation. This is what I can recall off the cuff because it's been quite a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00713. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, did certain elements of your command group provide security as well to certain facilities, and if so, which ones?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As is customary otherwise in peacetime, we behaved similarly during the aggression and the war. We secured our own parts first and foremost. By providing security for ourselves, we had an impact on general security in the town. We secured firstly and foremostly the buildings where we were; and in the general area of the town and the garrison, there were other facilities where we provided guards and other internal service organs as envisaged by the rules of service and a number of orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did members of your group also provide security for civilian facilities in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Members of our group, if civilian facilities were in question, provided security only to those facilities where parts of our group were, as well as parts of our garrison. So one could say that civilian facilities were secured as well because parts of our group were accommodated in such facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But once an army moves into a building, it is no longer a civilian building. I'm asking about hospitals or some such civilian facilities. Did you provide security to such facilities?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, not our group. Perhaps only indirectly, but not per establishment. For the most part, such facilities had their own security.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have D006-2528.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would it be convenient to have the break before or after? Now? We will do that. Could I remind you, Mr. Djurdjic, that we have received the transcript of evidence of the witness. Your opening summary concerned me. It seemed to me that you would be going into a great deal of detail. In view of the transcript and that this is a Rule 93 ter witness, we would ask that you concentrate on only matters of importance. Thank you. We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please have D006-2528.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It is your binder number 2, Mr. Filipovic. Perhaps you can even take out the document, it may be easier for you. Here we'll have an overview of manning levels in the Pristina Corps, the 28th of February, 1999. You signed this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to page 2 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the last column and the relation between the last two numbers there. What was the manning level that day?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This is one of the tables of the overview of manning levels of the Pristina Corps per branches and services. This only includes active-duty members of the Pristina Corps, that is to say, COs, NCOs, civilians, and soldiers under contract. Here we have soldiers split into two categories. There were those soldiers who were under an officer contract and other soldiers who were -- rank and file. We see that we had 779 soldiers that were originally requested, whereas the manning level on that day was 711. Next we have NCOs, the number required and the number available, and so on and so forth. In total, there should have been 4.471 active members, and at the time there were only 2.253. The manning level was then approximately around 50 per cent with active-duty members.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00714.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please go to document D006-2518 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is a document indicating the structure of losses in the Pristina Corps with its resubordinated units during the war. Can you tell us briefly something about this breakdown?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This is one of the indications of the losses of the Pristina Corps with resubordinated units. There are different approaches to indicating the number of losses. This is but one such possibility, and you can get brief insight into the losses themselves. Here we can see that 27 per cent of personnel were wounded, there were 3 per cent missing, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Killed, 27 per cent; missing, 3 per cent; and wounded, 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We can draw our own conclusions from this cake, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm just not clear what the basis for the information on that document is. It's a series of charts. But it's my submission we haven't seen a basis to be able to properly rely on the content of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. If there's some issue about it. Mr. Djurdjic, would you explore with the witness the source for the information on these charts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm trying to abide by your instructions. This document was in evidence in the Milutinovic case and explains the part of the transcript where the witness speaks about that topic. I didn't want to go into any further detail with this document because I believe it was sufficiently clarified in the previous transcript, but we may do so now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, let's go back to the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you rely upon the transcript, the document will be received. If Mr. Behar has some issue or concern, he can take that up in cross-examination, so carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00715.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, when the state of war was declared, what did the Pristina Corps Command do concerning its headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When the state of war was declared and when the NATO aggression began, the Pristina Corps resumed its work in keeping with the plans prepared beforehand and in keeping with parts of the mobilisation plan, much as all the other army units. The Pristina Corps Command moved from their peacetime location to a number of locations designated beforehand, and which were later on, depending on the situation, changed, because the Pristina Corps Command was simply forced to move out of the building where it used to be in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, from the moment when it moved at the beginning of the war to the end of the war, did the command ever return to the peacetime building used by the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From the moment it moved up until the end of the aggression, the command of the Pristina Corps never returned to the building and no one spent any time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the Pristina Corps building was empty during the war. Was it secured and who secured it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The building was secured, mainly from the outside, because there was a constant danger that it could be targeted by bombs. So that it was secured on the outside from quite a distance and the guards organs were in charge -- in charge of that in accordance with the rules of service. The commander of security was an officer named Vujovic who was deployed at the corps command in peacetime. He was in charge of physical education.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that the Pristina Corps Command was deployed in various locations. Please tell us whether any elements of the Pristina Corps Command were deployed at the Grand Hotel?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The Pristina Corps Command, as I said, was deployed out of the building where it stayed during peacetime from the beginning to the end of the NATO aggression. None of its elements were stationed at the Grand Hotel except for the fact that the information centre was located there. And that was also the place where mail was exchanged. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me whether the Grand Hotel was used as a hotel during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Grand Hotel played numerous roles. There were guests staying at the hotel, so were foreign and local journalists. There were also rooms that various private institutions had leased earlier on. The catering firm called Sloga [phoen] was also stationed there, and it worked without any problems throughout the work. The director of this company, Sloga was called Dragisa Vuckovic. There were also other institutions such as tourist agencies, and a branch of Kosmet Tours and many other organisations. They were also stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As the information centre was there, as you just said, and considering that this was a military element, was there any security of that part of the building, and who provided the security for the information centre?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The entire Grand Hotel and the information centre were secured. The hotel had its own security even before the information centre was established there. So the security performed their duty during the aggression as well. As far as I can remember, they stepped it up and they adapted it to war-time conditions. The personnel of the information centre also had their own internal security, which was covered by the internal service organs. Some of them were always on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was one of the functions of the military police to provide outside security of buildings and facilities?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Inter alia, as far as I can say, the military police also has the duty to provide security for the military facilities which it is charged with.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did Pristina Corps and 3rd Army commanders visit this place during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I do not have the information for the entire period of the aggression. I just remember that I visited, together with the Pristina Corps Commander. We once met at this information centre, and we toured it. That is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We'll talk about that later, Mr. Filipovic. But did commanders from the Pristina Corps or the 3rd Army, from any level, visit this information centre during the war, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That is possible, but I had my own duties and I do not really remember that well, so I could not say that with much certainty. It is possible, but what I do remember is the occasion when I visited it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there was outside security of the section of the Grand Hotel where the information centre was housed?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that there was security, yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You just mentioned that on one occasion you also visited the Grand Hotel. Can you tell us what that occasion was and what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. I think it was on the 28th of April. On the 27th of April, we had a meeting in the damaged building of the provincial Executive Council of Kosovo-Metohija. The meeting was attended by the corps commander and the 3rd Army commander; medals were awarded to a number of persons who had been decorated and who were from the Pristina Corps units. And after that meeting, the corps commander General Lazarevic talked to me and I proposed that he tour my command and the deployment of some elements of my command in Pristina. He told me that he was busy that day and that he would visit us the next day. That really happened; he visited my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me whether you had a role in this ceremony, and do you remember the time of the day when it was held on that day, the 27th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I could not say exactly what time it was, but it was day-time, somewhere around the middle of the day. I cannot remember the exact time, but it was daylight.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the 28th, how did the Pristina Corps Command visit your command? How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the corps commander came to the location where I was, that was very close to the Municipal Assembly of Pristina. He toured the parts of my command and groups which were stationed in that area. And, after that, we toured other parts of the command group and the garrison command. Among others, we also visited a part of the group which was stationed in cellars, that is to say, rather, the underground sections of the sports and cultural centre Boro i Ramiz. So we visited them. And, after that, we went to the Grand Hotel. There, we toured the information centre. So that was what happened on the 28th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Filipovic, how long were you together with the Pristina Corps Command on that day, the 28th of April?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it took quite a while. We were touring these parts of the command group for several hours. He was interested in many details. We --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, you've already told us that. Colonel, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Pristina in 1948, as I said. In the first residential block, in building number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where does your family originate from?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: My family originates from Kosovo and Metohija. My father was born in Gracanica next to the monastery, and my mother was born in Donja Cvracak in Vucitrn municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what is the distance between the city of Pristina and Gracanica?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: It is between 8 and 9 kilometres. It depends on the neighbourhood because Gracanica is quite big. But that's roughly the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to make a digression, were you a member of the collegium of the Pristina Corps before the war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the commanders collegium of the Pristina Corps for many years before the war. I was continuously a member since 1992. Moreover, I was the eldest member of the collegium because I was a member during four commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And when you were [as interpreted] appointed the head of the command group of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When I was appointed to the duty of the temporary commander of the Pristina garrisons and the head of the command group of the Pristina Corps, I occasionally attending the collegiums of the Pristina Corps, but sometimes the commander would call me even outside the times when the collegium would meet. So my presence was not as frequent at the time. It was just occasional.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let me ask you this as well, you told us how far Gracanica is from Pristina, but I also wish to ask you something about the control of territory in the city of Pristina and its environs. Was there any combat group stationed within the city of Pristina during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During the NATO aggression, as far as I remember, there was no combat group or any other combat unit of the Pristina Corps stationed in the city of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would go back to the military police now. Was there any military police in Pristina, and what were its tasks and duties in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember, the military police was mainly in charge of regulating traffic, primarily military traffic on the roads. Occasionally it also maintained law and order relating to members of the army because it participated in patrols. It also took part in on-site investigations when that was part of the duty of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me whether the administration of the Pristina military district had any units that were operating in Pristina, and what were their duties?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: There was a command of the Pristina military district and also a command of the Pristina military department. They were located in the barracks. The Pristina military department was subordinated to the military district command, and they had their military territorial units. These military territorial units, as far as I can remember, were deployed in the general area of responsibility from Podujevo to Strpci. In the general area of the Pristina garrison, there were military territorial units which, as far as I know, secured the territory and facilities mainly around the perimeter of the city of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was one of the duties of these military territorial units to secure military facilities and other special purpose facilities?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know, that was the duty of the military territorial units. At the time, that was one of their duties, to secure territory and specifically to secure facilities, which were of vital importance for the functioning of everyday life in this territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that your father was born in Gracanica. During the war in 1999, did you ever visit Gracanica?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm very familiar with the Gracanica village. I visited it during the aggression, that is to say, I toured that area for a number of reasons. One specific reason was that it was in the zone of responsibility of the Pristina garrison, and it is part of the Pristina municipality. Gracanica was the largest Serbian village, that is to say, the village that had the most numerous Serbian population in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. So I frequently visited Gracanica and the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, will you tell us in which periods you went to Gracanica, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give you the exact dates, but I think that since I was there several times, I was there towards the beginning and towards the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any civilians in Gracanica, and what was life like there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the population was there in Gracanica, and life was going on as normal, as much as possible in a situation of war. So war conditions affected all components of life. Shops did work, bakeries in Gracanica, the health centre, the post office, postal services were functioning, telegrams were received, citizens of Gracanica and from the villages of Ajvalija, Susice, Mramor, Slivovo, Dragovac received their pensions. Also Laplje Selo and so on. So life went on in Gracanica just as usual, although the area around Gracanica was bombed practically every day by NATO, especially the area of a warehouse that was about 500 to 1.000 metres from the centre of Gracanica. Perhaps it was a bit more than that, perhaps a kilometre and a half. Detonations were heard every day, but life went on unhindered as much as possible. Also there was traffic in the centre of Gracanica on the road between Pristina and Gnjilane that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, could you tell us something about your knowledge and your sources of knowledge regarding terrorist activities of the Albanian terrorist forces before the aggression started in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Before the aggression started, there were many terrorist attacks that were being committed by the Siptar terrorist forces. These attacks were numerous. The entire population of Pristina and the surrounding area lived in fear of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us first hear of what your knowledge was about the situation in the villages around the town of Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During the aggression or before the aggression?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Before the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, before the aggression, just like in the territory of the entire municipality of Pristina, in these villages there were numerous terrorist attacks. Practically there was not a single village where some terrorist attack had not been launched by the Siptar terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you have any specific examples that you could give us, and how come you know about these examples, if any?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Military facilities were attacked. Our warehouses in Sofalija, the warehouse right next to Gracanica, and police patrols were attacked, military vehicles that moved along these roads around Pristina. On the Podujevo-Pristina road near the Devet Jugovica barracks, the Siptar terrorists attacked a military vehicle and Colonel Cedomir Nikolic and Colonel Komordez [phoen] from the 3rd Army were seriously wounded there. They were fired at from the surrounding villages, from the area of Trudne and from the road leading to Prugovac and Grastica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether there were any kidnappings and killings from the villages that were there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: There were kidnappings and killings in the surrounding area, especially east of Gracanica, in the villages of Slivovo, Dragovac, then many villages that bordered with the territory the municipality of Pristina to the east of Gracanica, from the territory of Novo Brdo, Prekovce, Jasenovik.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have D006-2505 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Number 4 in your binder, Mr. Filipovic. This is a report of the 3rd Army Command, the security department, sent to the Supreme Command staff on the 13th of April, 1999. I would be interested in paragraph 3, if you can give us your comments on that. Did you have any knowledge in this regard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have an objection to the use of this document. In my submission, there's no basis for the admission of this document. And, in fact, this issue was dealt with in the Milutinovic case. And if I could, just with a brief indulgence, take Your Honours to that page. It's T-19167. I'm not sure, unfortunately, of the page number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The transcript that I've been provided with starts later than that page. It starts in the course of evidence and not at the beginning for some reason. It starts at page 19182.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I believe it's page 18 of D712.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since Ms. O'Leary gave me the beginning of the transcript, 19150 is the page that I have where Mr. Filipovic starts testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I think we do have the correct reference on the screen. Just to briefly outline the issue, Your Honour, this document relates to what an eye-witness allegedly saw. This issue was raised in the the Milutinovic case. The witness indicated at that time he had never seen this document until the proofing. And if you look at line 19 of the page we are currently on, His Honour Judge Bonomy asks the witness, What is this document? And the witness states: "It's a document, as can be seen, from the security department ..." And he indicates there an eye-witness is saying, again, as he will say now, that he was an eye-witness to the shooting of 20 Serbs. And the issue goes on, essentially the resolution in that case was that the Court would perhaps give it limited weight, but the exhibit was already in evidence. But that is not the case in this case. It's my submission that this witness has no basis to speak to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, again I tried to be faster. In the transcript we see that the witness did speak of this event, the one that is being referred to here. I just wanted him to give us his comments as to how come he knew about that event that is referred to in the transcript. I think that is important that he tells us what the source of his knowledge is regarding that event. Now, as to whether the document will be admitted or not, that is not the primary reason why I'm showing it now. There's going to be another witness through who I can tender this document. I want more knowledge about this document and what happened there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You certainly may explore briefly with the witness what he may know of an event. But it seems at the moment that you should not be putting the document to this witness. If you could proceed on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, you mentioned to us that there were kidnappings of non-Albanians before the war. I would like to ask you, since the transcript already says that you made such a statement, what is the source of your knowledge about what happened in the village of Marevce can you tell us what it was that you heard and how come you heard it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that in the broader area of the village of Marevce, there are many villages that had a Serb population. I had close relatives there and friend, and I visited them during my free time. These are the villages around Marevac: Gracanica, Slivovo, Dragovac, Brekovac, Zebince, Manicice [phoen], Trncevce [phoen], Klobukar, Izvor, Zebince, Bostane.
