In all these villages that I went to and where I met up with my close relatives, very close relatives and friends, many of them told me about family members of theirs who had gone missing. They were never found again. They went missing when they went into the field to till their land, when they went to the woods to chop some firewood. They never returned home. They never came back. There were many such cases in these villages that I mentioned, that is, the broader area of Marevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you do you know that the terrorists kidnapped and killed Albanians who were loyal to the state?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I am aware of such cases as well. They are generally known, if I can put it that way. I had direct knowledge about that at the time because I knew many people whom they had killed or kidnapped, who went missing. The media wrote about that too. I had concrete knowledge from that area, especially -- it especially affected those citizens who were loyal to the system and who did not fit into the terrorist policy of the Siptar terrorist forces. Many were liquidated, killed, they went missing, et cetera. In the broader area of the municipality of Pristina and even beyond.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what terrorist forces operated in the broader area of Pristina before the war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I do know. I heard about that at the collegium meetings of the corps commander, and I had personal knowledge as well from the field as I talked to citizens, citizens who were Siptars and Serbs and others. There were many terrorist forces in the area surrounding Pristina that was within the so-called operations zone lab. Operations zone lab is what it was called by the leaders of that Siptar terrorist movement. They had several brigades in that territory of the lab operations zone. Along the road between Pristina and Podujevo, the 141st, the 151st, the 152nd, the 153rd, the 154th Siptar Terrorist Brigade; and they had their own centres, two centres, basically command posts from where they gave orders to these units, the east of Gracanica and Pristina, in the broader area of Zlas, Marevac, Kukavica, Mramor; their headquarters were in Zlas and in the broader area, or, rather, to the north-east of Pristina in the broader area of Makovac, Karcikovo [phoen], Grastica, Kolic --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: -- were there headquarters in Grastica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, in the town of Pristina itself, were you aware of any activities of Albanian terrorists on the eve of the war in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the eve of the aggression, or, rather, before the aggression, there were many acts of terrorism that were committed. There were many terrorist attacks against the civilian population, Serb and Siptar. Shops, catering establishments within Pristina itself and on the outskirts of Pristina. There were quite a few of them, and they were evident, even considerably, before the aggression. However, they became more intensified as the aggression was getting closer. There was a countless number of them; I cannot even remember all of them. But some were particularly striking because of the way in which they were carried out. And that is what I remember particularly. Military columns that were moving along roads, policemen, police patrols around Pristina; there were bloody attacks with bloody consequences. Four policemen got killed practically in the centre of Pristina in the street of Miladin Popovic. They were fired at from a vehicle and all four of them got killed in the middle of Pristina. The terrorists drove away after having killed them. I passed there just before this event took place, or, rather, just after it happened, and I saw the blood there. Then in Prijevo [phoen] and in the area of the clinical centre on the road between Pristina and Lipljan towards Caglavica two policemen were killed and one was seriously wounded. They were fired at from houses. They were attacked by hand-grenades and rifles. There were many other attacks, terrorist acts, and they were registered in different documents and reports. It's a generally known thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Filipovic. After the war began, do you know of any terrorist activities in the town itself, and if so, where did you get that information?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: There were numerous terrorist activities in the town itself including the entire duration of the aggression and after the Kumanovo Agreement. Such occurrences still take place. In particular, they usually came from Vranjevac. It is a densely populated neighbourhood in Pristina where the terrorists enjoyed a wide support. That part of Pristina also represented their logistics base for the functioning of the operational staff of operations zone, Lap. Then, also, there was a part of Maticane, it is a neighbourhood in the outskirts of Pristina, gravitating towards the general area of the clinical centre. Next, the area of Dragodan where the American information centre was housed; it is a neighbourhood to the north-west of the railway station in Pristina. There were such events in the very centre of Pristina as well where citizens were killed, kidnapped, and their bodies later found in the town itself as well as around the town, particularly in the area of Zatric Potok, which is along the railroad and the road from Pristina towards Vranjevac and Medvedje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, could you tell us what the situation was in Pristina and its environs as of the beginning of the aggression, in terms of air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The town of Pristina and its environs were constantly being attacked by NATO aircraft. They also attacked the town itself, including its old part and the general area of the garrison and the municipality of Pristina. It was incessant during the day, night, in the morning, in the afternoon, on national holidays, religious holidays, and during Easter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have document D007-4429.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 7. This is a report about NATO aggression on the 24th and 25th April, 1999, by the provincial information centre. Colonel, did you receive such reports, and where was this provincial information centre housed?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I did receive such reports, reports on NATO aggression on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. In such reports there were also incidents of attack recorded in Pristina and its environs; such reports were drawn up by the defence directorate or administration, the seat of which was in Pristina. Such reports were compiled based on data received from, among others, the provincial information centre in charge of the municipality of Pristina. It was housed in the immediate vicinity of my command, in the municipal building. Saric Vuksan [phoen] and Dopuco Mico [phoen] were at the helm of the centre; I received their oral and written reports pertaining to the town of Pristina and the results of bombardment as well as other kinds of events in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I must object, once again, to the use of this document for similar reasons. There is a threshold issue and that is that I think it's apparent just even on a brief look that the translation we have is not complete. But the core of my concern is that, once again, it's not clear what the connection is between this document and the witness. This was also explored in the Milutinovic case. And if I could draw your attention to page 22 of the D712.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't have numbered pages in that order and nor do I have the complete transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Perhaps if it's brought on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- so something seems to have gone wrong. What was the page, the transcript page number?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: It's T-9171. It's now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't have that. I start later than that page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the reason for that is. That is -- the version I have does include that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be looked at during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Maybe if I can just work off of the copy that's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: At line 20, and this is in reference to the same document, Judge Bonomy had asked: "What is the connection, your connection to this document, Mr. Filipovic?" Continuing on the next page, if we could see the following page. At line 3, Judge Bonomy asks: "So this is a report to you, albeit it says the 3rd Army?" And the answer was: "No, no, this report was not submitted to me. It was submitted by the operations centre of the civilian protection, and they had this information." Counsel is asked at line 16 if this was Mr. Filipovic's report. He states: "It is not." And then Judge Bonomy inquiries as to why he is being asked about it. And just to complete that, if we look on the following page, which is 19173, at line 2, Judge Bonomy states: " -- he has got no familiarity with it. He hasn't told us that he was there and saw the bombing take place and can confirm it. So we haven't advanced matters by actually spending time in court and exploring this orally." In my submission, that -- this document, and this, in fact, applies to a number of similar documents that my friend may intend to use, but there is not the sufficient connection between this witness and these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what refers to the period of time mentioned here goes for our document number 5498, a Pristina Corps Command document sent to the 3rd Army. Among other targets, there was a warehouse and a factory hit in Pristina. The witness was asked about that as well. I asked the witness whether he received such reports, and confirmed that, indeed, he received such reports of air-strikes from the centre. I intentionally skipped over a couple of documents which were combat reports of the Pristina Corps because there was some discussion about that in the previous proceedings about whether he was present and what was his source of knowledge. As for this document, he received information and reports from the provincial centre. Those documents became part of evidence in the Milutinovic case, alongside all the other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying that you would advance this on the basis that, at the time, he was aware of this document, as it was prepared not by him but by another independent organisation, but it was known to him at the time? Are you saying that he knows anything of the matters that are dealt with in the document from his own observation and knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there are several elements here. One is that witness himself provided information used to compile such reports. Another element is that this is information about Pristina. And he was familiar with it -- that information. The service processing information received information from the witness and then sent reports to him. That is why the witness is familiar with this document, and I believe he said so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It may be one thing, Mr. Djurdjic, if the witness gave information that is set out in the document that you want him to consider; two, the organisation that prepared a report, and he then later saw the report. At the moment, though, I've not heard that this witness had any personal knowledge of any event that is set out in this report. Is there something there that you can follow up?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We'll clear that right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, we opened the document which is your tab number 7. What is there in the contents of this document, just briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to be as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So what is the subject of the report?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In this report, one can see a number of cases pertaining to Pristina, such as explosions that I could hear myself. There are such entries here. For example, four explosions in the surroundings of Pristina, then two explosions between Slatina and Gorazde. The entire Pristina could hear such explosions; five explosions in the area of Golac, we see what the time was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, Mr. Filipovic. It says here which parts of Pristina were bombed and when?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Out of the data that has to do with Pristina, was there any information that your service provided?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we kept co-operating with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you receive such information sent to reports for your perusal?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: My garrison affairs organ received it, and I provided information concerning Pristina to the information centre. We were basically in the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's fine. But was this as part of your command group, did the command group officially receive such reports?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I seek your instruction. Do you want me to tender this document, or should I only focus on the information contained therein that has to do with Pristina and discuss it with the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The document appears to be one that is of only remote relevance to the operations of the garrison unit commanded by the witness. He does not suggest any personal knowledge of the contents of the document other than perhaps that he could hear explosions. For those reasons, the Chamber would not be persuaded that this document ought to be received. In addition to that, there is the problem that clearly we do not have a full translation. But I wanted to deal with the substance of the matter, and that is that on the present evidence we do not see any sufficient basis to receive this document through this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, the chief of the defence administration, Mr. Petar Ilic, what is that organisation?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Petar Ilic was the chief of the defence administration. That organisation, in terms of hierarchy, was under the Ministry of Defence. He was subordinated to the republican defence administration and the republican defence administration in turn to the Federal Ministry of Defence. He, however, had municipal centres subordinated to him. In the municipalities they were reporting an alarming centres [as interpreted]. And based on the constitution and the Law on Armed Forces, as well as the Law on Defence, we were duty-bound to co-operate with them. Mr. Ilic hailed from Suvi Do from Pristina, and I frequently met with him in addition to knowing him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We see here that that service kept record of all air-strikes, for example, the night between the 24th and 25th of April. What can we see here? When was Pristina bombed during that period and where?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The 21st and the 22nd of May, there were one, two, three, four --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, what is the witness referring to? He seems to be reading something. What is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the document I showed him where we have the times and locations of air-strikes. I don't know, Your Honour, why ... there are some documents with incomplete translations, but, later on, we seem to have a full translation in English. For some reason unknown to me, we only have the end of this document here. There must have been a mistake. This temporal overview of air-strikes for the whole day, for the entire territory, and I wanted only to present to the witness those portions which had to do with Pristina and its environs and to ask him about that, whether he had specific knowledge concerning some events. That was my goal, and that is why I chose to present these documents. And I thought the translations which were not complete - and I keep record of it, such as this one which is incomplete - I wanted to have them only marked for identification pending translation. It is unclear to me why this was translated in such a way. And what do we have at the end of the document? We have Pristina and public utility services and what they were like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, we have ruled that we do not receive this document. It should not be used, therefore, to prompt the memory or the evidence of the witness. If you want to explore with him his knowledge of air-strikes on a particular day or in a particular period, you may do so, but not with the assistance of this document. Is that clear enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness seems to have the document in front of him and to be constantly referring to it. That should not occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please skip all the documents in your binder up until 16, and then I will tell you what you will skip after that, because these documents relate to --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I've skipped everything up to number 16 just as you told me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's right. And then I'm tell you what you are going to skip after that. Tell me what your specific knowledge is regarding the bombing of Pristina and the surrounding area until the break-out of the war in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: My knowledge related to the bombing of Pristina and the surrounding area is vast. It would take a long time for me to describe all these attacks even in the briefest possible terms, and that is what I'll try to do. I said that Pristina was bombed at all times, day and night. There is information about that, and I personally witnessed that. Furthermore, facilities in the centre of Pristina, also on the outskirts of Pristina and beyond. The bus station in Pristina was totally destroyed. The transformer station was bombed in the town of Pristina, and many transmission lines and installations in Pristina were damaged, and, therefore, Pristina had no power for days. Also, the post office was bombed along with telephone and telegraph installations in the centre of Pristina. Then the Orthodox cemetery --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can we just stop at this point a bit. Since you mentioned the post office, do you perhaps remember the date when that facility was bombed?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were many days like that, but that left a lasting imprint in my memory because it reminded me of the bombing of Belgrade on the 6th of April, 1941, when the Second World War started.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see video D006-2504.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we play it further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you are familiar with this footage that we saw. Tell me, what was that building that we saw in this footage?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That was the post office, the post office and the telecom building in the very centre of Pristina. NATO projectiles hit the post office building, then they also hit the building of the pension fund, the social insurance and pension funds in Pristina. Also they hit a few houses near the post office that were levelled to the ground. The people who lived in these houses got killed and were seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you on the spot when this explosion occurred and when this damage was sustained?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I was relatively nearby so I went to the scene immediately. I took part in the rescue endeavour, trying to help the wounded. The organs of my command were carrying out the dead and wounded. Civilian protection organs took part in this too. The commander of the civil protection of the province can be seen in this footage. Also, the police organs took part in the rescue operation and in putting out the fire. Many shops and restaurants were damaged. Supermarkets, for example, the supermarket that was owned by a certain Rajko, and then Dragan Nikolic, who owned a restaurant, had his restaurant destroyed --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, we're waiting for a convenient pause. Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have an objection to the the use of the video as well, and, at the risk of sounding like a broken record here, I don't have an issue with the witness discussing what he saw, the observations that he made; but, in my submissions, it's completely unclear, to begin with, who shot this video, how it was shot, when it was shot, who edited it together - and you can see just on the short portion that we observed there are a number of clips that are put together - it's not clear how they were edited or why. In my submission, in the absence of clear information with respect to the video, then the video itself is not proper to be put to the witness. I should add just one additional point. An additional concern with putting exhibits like this to the witness first is, of course, that it may be seen to be putting things, leading of a sort, putting things into the mouth of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a clip that was used in the Milutinovic case. I did not think ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will receive the video, Mr. Behar, in keeping with its practice over many videos and photographs in this -- the trial, many of which have been tendered by the Prosecution. The point you make that the evidence of a witness may be prompted by seeing a video is valid and it is an issue which we watch. And in the circumstances of this case, in respect of this video, the Chamber is not concerned that there has been any significant issue about the reliability of the general content of the video. So it will be received as an exhibit, despite the objection. And you can carry on, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00716.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, did the members of your command group take part in this? Did they help after the bombing that we saw just now?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The members of the command group of the command of the corps took part in saving the wounded, helping them, carrying out the dead, et cetera. Many people took part, like Sergeant Dobrivoje Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like us to go back to this subject, but it's not between the 6 and the 7th. What do you know, if anything, in relation to the bombing of the area surrounding Pristina? Did you tour any of the places that had been affected?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The surroundings of Pristina were intentionally bombed, just like the centre of Pristina. Pristina and its surrounding area was bombed all the time. Since this was the territory of the Pristina garrison that I was in charge of, both my organs and I toured the area frequently. It was the village of Sufalija that was bombed, the broader area. Then the broader area of Gornja Brnjica, Donja Brnjica, Devet Jugovica, then the village of Gracanica, then the Kisnica water works that supplied Pristina with water. That is why the citizens of Pristina often had no water, and bread production was imperilled as well, although attempts were made to keep it regular. Then the transmission lines in the broader area of Pristina were bombed, especially in the area of Donja Brnjica, Devet Jugovica, and Mazgita. I personally came across the teams that were trying to repair the damage sustained. The teams that were repairing transmission lines were mixed teams consisting of Serbs and Siptars. Many Siptars figured prominently in terms of their bravery, and later on they were decorated and awarded for their efforts. I can give you their names as well, some of the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In terms of the position that you held, did you also go to neighbourhoods that were outside the city centre?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I often went to neighbourhoods that were outside town to see elements that belonged to my garrison to gain immediate knowledge as to what was going on so that I could take further measures within the garrison in order to make it possible to have the most bearable life possible, because the bombing took place every day, all the time. I can tell you which places I visited and what I observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information about -- about what was used in the bombing? What kind of equipment?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I had a lot of information. I had practically daily insight. I can document many things from that field, particularly the fact that the broader area of Pristina was bombed with projectiles that contained depleted uranium. Then cluster bombs were also used, as well as projectiles that caused various chemical effects, that is to say, their use led to what is termed chemical accidents, especially because of the bombing of a plant in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how come you know that bombs containing depleted uranium were used?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I received information from the units that were in the broader area of the garrison of Pristina and in the actual area of the Pristina garrison that were in charge of establishing that and measuring levels of radiation. For example, elements of the 52nd ABiH Battalion that were deployed in the area of my garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you on the scene, yourself, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. And I even did some things that were untoward, and I regret that to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where were you when you say that you were on the scene?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Gornja Brnjica. I was in Donja Brnjica. I was in the area facing Grmija, above the former teacher's college in Sofalija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You are giving me answers that are too extensive and not responsive to my questions. I asked you about the location where you were where depleted uranium was used, and how come you know?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I caught these projectiles with my own hands in the area of Donja Grmija. That is the untoward thing that I did. And I brought them to Pristina so that all citizens could see them. And, to this day, I suffer the effects of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were measures taken at these locations where this was used?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In that area -- in those areas, measures were taken that are prescribed for the units of the army and of the civilian protection, as well as other defence structures. That is to say that signs were put up from the regular kits, marking the areas where the projectiles were fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that it is the right time for the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, we resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, before the war and throughout the war you were in Pristina, if I understood you well?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I was in Pristina between 1986 and until the end of the war, that is to say, the 29th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any knowledge whether just before the war there were any mass movements or leaving of the population from Pristina and its environs?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the eve of the aggression against our country and the bombardment, there were people moving out from Pristina itself, and its general area. Siptars were moving out, Serbs, Roma, Turks, and all those who resided there. There were such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Because I saw it with my own eyes. Those citizens moving away, some of them worked with me, others worked with members of my family, lived in the same apartment blocks. We were neighbours. I have that knowledge from daily life.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did the people you talked to specify any reasons for leaving Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did say why. Basically all ethnicities had the same reasons. There were several reasons. The first and most important one was the looming threat of bombardment. That is something they were expecting to happen. In foreign media, this was widely reported, as well as in some domestic media. There were also rumours travelling between people and they told me they wanted to move away because they feared for their families and children in particular. It was also because of Siptar terrorist attacks which grew in frequency. There was an upward trend before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall any specific conversations with people?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I do. I remember many. Before the aggression, I spoke with those who wanted to move their families outside Pristina and Kosovo-Metohija. Some of them were Serbs, others were Siptar, and these were the reasons they usually mentioned, that they were fearful of the looming air-strikes and terrorist attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about after the beginning of the air campaign? Were there people still moving out, and what do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in brief, I had numerous such experiences, and it took place for a number of reasons. As of the 24th of March onwards, air-strikes began and in certain periods such strikes occurred more frequently than in others. Both Serbs and Siptars were moving away. It particularly escalated after repeated bombardment of the town of Pristina itself as well as its centre and its postal building and other buildings destroyed around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that because I spoke to many citizens. I also could feel that myself. There were no telephone lines. After the telecom facility was destroyed, perhaps only 20 per cent of all communication still worked. There were different power cuts because power lines and generator stations were bombed in Pristina and its environs. On a number of occasions, Pristina went completely dark because of the gases, fumes, and smoke caused because the Jugopetrol company's warehouse was destroyed in the general area of Pristina at Devet Jugovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember specific people with whom you discussed this?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I do. I spoke with Vasilije Grbic; with his neighbours, Siptars; with Tomislav Milenkovic, who was a well-known math professor from Pristina who left. He left his apartment keys to his neighbour who was a Siptar. He even gave him his fridge and entrusted him with his dog for safekeeping just before moving away. I spoke with Branko Brudar who had intended to move his family out. And once on their way, he moved them to Montenegro. And, as a matter of fact, his child was killed at Morina because that's a where a NATO aircraft struck when his family was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you speak with any Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: With many. In particular with those who were in columns passing by my command post and by the building where part of my command was. As they were moving in the column, I asked them, Where are you going? Why? You needn't go. They said, We are leaving; we were told to do so; and we, ourselves, are not really clear why we have to leave. I frequently saw them close to my command post. They would go back and forth and on one day and the next.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It is not clear to me. You are now talking about some people who passed by your command on several occasions but they didn't leave?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that problem of moving away is a complex issue, and it is difficult to explain it. There were people moving away before and during the aggression. Then there were those who moved and came back a number of times, both Siptars and Serbs. There were people who tried to create a feeling that they were moving away and they would circle Pristina and then go back to their houses. There were quite a number of such people. They usually passed by my command. They would go one way and then return. And they would do this on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You've just explained that, thank you. You have mentioned that there was a separate category of people who first moved away and then returned to their places of residence. How do you know that, and what kind of category is this? Please be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Those who left Kosovo and Metohija and Pristina itself were also of different ethnicities, Serbs, Siptar. During the aggression, people were particularly trying to have their children move away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, please be specific. You mentioned a category of people who moved away and then returned. How did that come about? Please explain.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll give you an example. In the village of Ajvalija, which is on the outskirts of Pristina and is populated mainly by Albanians, at the time, there were between 4- and 5.000 Albanians and some 2- to 300 Serbs. They lived together without any problem, save for their great fear of bombardment because a part of their village was bombed. And, at some point in time, the Siptars began moving away towards Mramor next to the Gracanac lake and across Vujic Potok or stream. We asked them why they were leaving and they said, Well, we were told to go there, to go to Mramor, and that the accommodation would be provided and we would be supplied with everything we needed. Four or five days later when no one received them there, most of them returned to Ajvalija, and they stayed there until the end of the aggression, although, some of them did not return for the fear of bombardment. Basically, the village was bombed and its environs from all sides, especially in the area where there used to be a mine close to Ajvalija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that there were some calls for the population to move out?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recall those. I even remember there was a flier that one could frequently come across in the streets of Pristina. Some members of my command and garrison found leaflets like that. They were in the Albanian language, inviting Albanians to move away towards Albania and Macedonia because there was allegedly going to be a large offensive of the Serb police and military, and because of the inability of the terrorist forces to protects them, as well as that the NATO pact, which they asked to help them, would be unable to protect them at that point in time. That is what the leaflet said. Fear was spread in different ethnic communities by way of leaflets that were thrown out of NATO airplanes. These leaflets had terrifying pictures of the super bombarder B-52 NATO aircraft with those aircraft being shown as dropping bombs. And underneath in the picture there was a civilian population. It says that there would be carpet bombing from these super flying fortresses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that there was a category of people who moved out. Did you discuss this with any of those people? Did they tell you why they were leaving? And I'm particularly interested in whether you had any contact with any members of the Albanian community.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I had frequent contact with them. I spoke to a certain Redzep, with a certain Fado, a Dzemo. I used to know them from the Territorial Defence. Some of them were my work-mates, while others were acquaintances from the town. I even attended some schools together in Pristina with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what were the reasons they specified for leaving Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, mostly they said that they were afraid and that they didn't know how long these air-strikes would last. They said they feared for their families and children in particular and that they were afraid of Siptar terrorist actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were in Pristina throughout that period. Did you see or do you have any knowledge of the army and the police exercising pressure on the Albanian population and telling them that they should move?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The army and police never exerted any pressure. They never told the population to leave. Quite the contrary. The army and police took all measures to avoid that. I know certain measures that were taken which insisted on our personal conduct and personal example so as to try to persuade people to stay. We were supposed to talk to them and behave properly so that they would stay. We were there to stabilise conditions and offer resistance to Siptar terrorists and to secure the functioning of services in the town, although there were power cuts and sometimes there was no water, there was destruction, and the population was frequently injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please now have D011-2339. Before that, I ask for your leave, Your Honours, to have this map added on to the 65 ter list of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I can just indicate I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Behar. Yes, that will be added to the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we zoom in on the central part. A bit more. Scroll down, please. I apologise, scroll up. More, more, that's right. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, on this map, can you indicate where Lapska Street is?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'll have a look. I think I might be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please mark it as 1.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where is the market, the bazaar, the old market, that is?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see Kojlovica on this map; in which direction is it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The bazaar, can you mark it with 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Kojlovica is this way, this way. So you follow Proleterska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mark it with a K. For Kojlovica.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You said it is in this direction. From Lapska Street, can you see Kojlovica?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The village of Kojlovica cannot be seen from Lapska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Because between Lapska Street and Kojlovica there is no line of sight because of the lie of the land and buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the distance between the location you marked as 1 and the village of Kojlovica?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: There should be between 3 and 5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you indicate where the Vranjevacki Bridge is?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please mark it with 3.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, during the war, did you see any tanks or armoured vehicles on that bridge?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I visited that area a few times during the war. And whenever I did, there were never any tanks there. Also, people from my command who moved about the area also told me that there was not a single tank or armoured combat vehicle there throughout the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the town of Pristina during the war, did you see any armoured vehicles or tanks at all irrespective of whose those vehicles were?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the town of Pristina, I didn't see any. There were no armoured vehicles or tanks there. They were not there during the aggression. The 15th Armoured Brigade, the seat of which in the Kosovski Junaci barracks part, of their units were there and some of them were at the Pristina airport, but they had actually moved out before the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where was that tank unit, in what barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: It was on the outskirts of Pristina along the road between Pristina and Kosovo Polje to the right of that road vis-à-vis the agricultural school to the west of the Orthodox cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the Vranjevac hill, you marked the bridge, is there a barracks on that hill where there may have been armoured vehicles or tanks?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the Vranjevac hill, there were no barracks. And there were no tanks or armoured combat vehicles or artillery pieces for that matter. No military group was deployed there for several reasons. First of all, Vranjevac is densely populated and the streets are exceptionally narrow because no urban planning was applied. In that settlement, there were numerous terrorist groups and the logistics of the Lap operations zone of the Siptar terrorists. These were the main reasons why. There was not a tank there or any combat assets of the army, there was only a police station which was there in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where is Lukare? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Lukare --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. If you cannot see it, just tell us you cannot see it, but you can show us the general direction.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Lukare is in this direction here. This is what I'm going to do now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And how far away is Lukare from the location that you marked with number 1?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Lukare is about, well, say 2 or 3 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just tell us, or, rather --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the transcript to reflect that the witness marked the direction where Lukare is, and he wrote Lukare in his own hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In view of the terrain, can you tell us whether from location number 1 a person can see the village of Lukare?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, it is not possible. From Lapska Street, you cannot see Lukare. No way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And right now, on this map, do we see where the Orthodox cemetery is in Dragodan?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: It should be evident, but could the the map be scrolled down about 5 centimetres?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not without losing the markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just take it slowly, Mr. Filipovic, let us see.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: It would have to go up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, we are now going to admit this map so that we don't lose any of the markings, and then we are going to show you the map again.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What you can see here is the Islamic cemetery and --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Take it easy. Just slowly, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please tender this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00717.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have the same document again, the map without any markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now we can see Lapska Street and Dragodan and the cemetery, Mr. Filipovic. Is the map positioned --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we can try to zoom it in again.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. No need to zoom in. Let me see. I see Lapska Street, yes, but now the cemetery -- it has to go up a bit. A bit up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll down a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A bit more. That's right. Now the cemetery can be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, again, could you mark Lapska Street and put number 1 there.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Number 1 is Lapska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, the railway station in Pristina, could you put a circle around it.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And number 2, please. Could you place number 2 there by the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And now could you put a circle around the cemetery at Dragodan.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And place number 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, from location number 1, can a person see location number 3?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, it is impossible. It is impossible. From Lapska Street you cannot see the Orthodox cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00718.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, I'm now going to present a witness statement here of a witness who was heard here, Ms. Nazalie Bala. Could you please tell me, during her testimony in court, and the transcript reflects this, Ms. Bala said that she saw check-points because she worked in Dragodan, she said, I worked at the RC Pristina that is behind the former American office. The check-point was right by the American office; the other check-point was as Dragodan Bridge; and the third in Tophane, that links the old and new parts of town. I would like to ask you whether there were check-points, to the best of your knowledge, at these locations after the war broke out in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During the aggression, I moved about very often through the town of Pristina. Parts of my units moved about frequently as they were carrying out their tasks too. I never saw a check-point in the town of Pristina, and no one from their ranks ever reported to me about the existence of a check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. She also said that at the main entry points to Pristina from Gnjilane, Skopje, Prizren, and Podujevo, there were check-points with barbed wire. Did you tour these locations, and are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I went to all of those places several times and there was no barbed wire there or any kind of obstacles to the movement of the population or vehicles. Not at a single exit or entry road in the town of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If checks were carried out at some positions by the police or military, were they carried out vis-à-vis all the persons who were in transit on that particular road?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Those checks were carried out in respect of all persons regarding all the citizens of Pristina and the surrounding area and whoever passed by, irrespective of ethnicity and irrespective of occupation. As a matter of fact, checks were carried out both by the police and the military police. So very often we would also stop the police, and the police would stop us. Once we would show our IDs and establish who we were, then we would continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Bala also says, When I looked in the direction of Dragodan from my terrace, I saw the police forces as they were moving in armoured vehicles, trucks, and other vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From there she could not see that. Her building was rather high, but she could not see what she said that she saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As you moved about Pristina, did you see armoured vehicles and tanks, either military or police vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I did not see a single armoured vehicle ever. A military armoured vehicle or a police armoured vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In her statement and in the transcript, Ms. Bala says that around 1400 hours on the 28th of March she heard and saw the shelling of Kojlovica, a neighbourhood in Pristina, and that she saw the Serb artillery firing from Vranjevac towards Kojlovica.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: She could never see any Serb artillery at Vranjevac because, quite simply, it never was there. It is well known where the Pristina Corps units were. Exactly so. And since that was my area of responsibility, the garrison of Pristina, I know that there was no artillery. And there couldn't have been any artillery for that. Even if somebody wanted to deploy artillery there, that would be in contravention of all tactical rules. Also it is impossible because the streets are so narrow and houses are right next to one another because this neighbourhood was built up outside proper urban planning. Also, there was a large concentration of Siptar terrorist groups in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Bala says, on page 2341 of the transcript, line 22 and line 23, and then 24 and 25 as well, that she saw a tank firing in the village of Lukare, firing from a hill there towards the hill of Kojlovica.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the village of Lukare she could not see a single tank because there weren't any there. In the village of Lukare, there was just a military depot that was bombed all the time. It was bombed almost every single day. That depot was bombed all the time. And strong detonations were heard. In other parts of town, some glass on windows was shattered because the detonations there. There weren't any combat vehicles -- armoured combat vehicles there during the aggression, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you something else. From the 26th of March onwards, did you ever see or hear or receive any reports to the effect that the army and the police were expelling the Albanian population?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Never. I never heard of that. I never saw that kind of expulsion, or could that have happened in respect to the tasks that we receive. If something like that happened on an individual basis, and I never observed any such thing, such a person would certainly have charges brought against him in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: My last question, Mr. Filipovic. Did you ever hear that in Pristina and the surrounding area there were paramilitary formations during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Never. During the course of the aggression there was not a single paramilitary organisation either in Pristina or in the surrounding area or any individual who behaved in a paramilitary way. I did not notice anyone like that, and I have no information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Filipovic. Thank you, Your Honours, I've just completed my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. The statement you quoted from, that is an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. P420. Bala, Nazalie's statement, dated the 30th of June, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We must adjourn now. As there is a Plenary sitting of Judges tomorrow, we will have to continue the trial on Friday. We commence at 10.00, and we'll sit through until 4.00. So, I am sorry, sir, but we must ask you to return on Friday morning at 10.00 to continue your evidence. A Court Officer will show you out after we rise. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
